title: Pulsar Science with the SKA Observatory
extended_summary:
This paper is a lead article for a special issue on pulsar science with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO). It does not study an educational intervention or K-12 science-learning outcome; instead, it surveys the planned capabilities of the SKA-Low and SKA-Mid telescopes and explains how these instruments are expected to transform pulsar and neutron-star research.

The article focuses on the observatory’s observing frequency ranges, sensitivity, beamforming, timing, and search subsystems, and then summarizes the companion papers in the special issue. It describes how these technical capabilities will support multiple science cases, including pulsar censuses, globular-cluster pulsars, Galactic-centre pulsars, neutron-star population studies, pulsar magnetospheres, Galactic plasma and magnetic fields, pulsar wind nebulae, tests of gravity, neutron-star interiors, and pulsar timing arrays.

The context is astrophysical rather than educational: the paper discusses the SKAO’s AA* and AA4 rollout stages and how they will enable new discoveries over the coming decade. Its main conclusion is that the SKAO’s large sensitivity, broad frequency coverage, and flexible multi-beam operation will be a transformative facility for pulsar science and fundamental physics, but it does not report empirical study results, participant outcomes, or implementation data relevant to K-12 education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a domain science review/position-style article about SKA pulsar astronomy, not an empirical K-12 education study. It does not evaluate an educational intervention, does not report a study design for student outcomes, and provides no education-relevant causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 educational impact is demonstrated or measured. The paper concerns future astrophysics capabilities, so there is no direct evidence of effect on learner outcomes or educational systems.

finding.finding_summary: This paper argues that the SKA Observatory will substantially strengthen scientific reasoning capabilities in astronomy and astrophysics by enabling much larger and more precise pulsar datasets. It projects that the SKA will more than double the known pulsar population (e.g., ~10,000 slow pulsars and nearly 800 MSPs in AA*; >12,000 total in AA4), which would improve inference about neutron-star evolution, gravity, plasma physics, and dense-matter properties, but these are forecasted science capabilities rather than measured educational outcomes.
finding.measure: Projected scientific discovery capacity and inferred advances in astrophysical reasoning; no educational measure reported
